newsitem.title: USA: Time Warner's Atlantic Group cuts workforce.
newsitem.headline: Time Warner's Atlantic Group cuts workforce.

text.p: Time Warner Inc's Atlantic Group music division said Wednesday it has cut some staff to streamline its operations.
Company officials declined to provide further details, but industry sources said the division was cutting as much as 13 percent of its workforce, which totals about 500 people.
"It is a sad day indeed when we have to say goodbye to people who have made valuable contributions to the life of this great company," Atlantic said in a statement.
"We have reshaped The Atlantic Group with one goal in mind -- to create a streamlined, exceptional team in response to the volatile state of the music marketplace today," it said.
Industry sources also said the company was planning to consolidate several of Atlantic's labels and slash several artists from its roster.
One source close to the company attributed the cuts to Atlantic's new co-Chairman Val Azzoli, who is seeking to trim costs and overhead.
Many people in the industry were not surprised by the moves, saying that Atlantic's overhead has long been considered to be bloated.

"This is common in the music industry. Problems tend to accumulate as middle management is reluctant to let people go until problems increase, and then they have to cut more people all at once," said Thomas White, an artist rights expert.
Atlantic has faced several setbacks recently, such as disappointing sales by Hootie & the Blowfish, one of its most high-profile acts.
But sources familiar with the situation insist there was no connection between Hootie and the announced cutbacks.
They said Atlantic will drop as many as 50 other bands and artists from its roster by early next year.
Despite some problems, Atlantic has led all other record labels in recent weeks.

"Atlantic has been the No. 1 label in current market share for six out of the past eight weeks, and the changes we have made ensure that we will remain at the forefront of the industry for many years to come."
In addition to Atlantic, Time Warner owns several other record groups, including Warner Brothers and Electra.
